claim: New neurons generated in the postnatal ventricular–subventricular zone (V-SVZ) migrate to the olfactory bulb (OB) through the rostral migratory stream (RMS), forming elongated aggregates called chains.
source: New neurons generated in the postnatal ventricular–subventricular zone (V-SVZ) migrate to the olfactory bulb (OB) through the rostral migratory stream (RMS), forming elongated aggregates called chains (Doetsch and Alvarez-Buylla, 1996; Lois et al., 1996; Lois and Alvarez-Buylla, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Doetsch and Alvarez-Buylla, 1996; Lois et al., 1996; Lois and Alvarez-Buylla, 1994) that established this phenomenon.

claim: Within the OB, new neurons migrate individually and radially and terminate their migration in the granule cell layer (GCL) or glomerular layer (GL), where they are differentiated into GABAergic interneurons and incorporated into the OB neural circuit.
source: Within the OB, new neurons migrate individually and radially and terminate their migration in the granule cell layer (GCL) or glomerular layer (GL), where they are differentiated into GABAergic interneurons and incorporated into the OB neural circuit (Bressan and Saghatelyan, 2020; Kaneko et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bressan and Saghatelyan, 2020; Kaneko et al., 2017).

claim: Both chain-forming and individually migrating neurons use blood vessels as physical scaffolds for their migration in the RMS and OB.
source: Previous studies have shown that both chain-forming and individually migrating neurons use blood vessels as physical scaffolds for their migration in the RMS and OB (Bovetti et al., 2007; Snapyan et al., 2009; Whitman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bovetti et al., 2007; Snapyan et al., 2009; Whitman et al., 2009).

claim: GFP+ new neurons interact closely with blood vessels in the RMS, GCL, external plexiform layer, and GL.
source: The results showed that GFP+ new neurons interact closely with blood vessels in the RMS, GCL, external plexiform layer, and GL (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—video 2; Figure 1—videos 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-D and associated videos.

claim: In the RMS and GL, the majority of new neurons were present within 5 µm of the inner surface of vessels.
source: In particular, in the RMS and GL, the majority of cells were present within 5 µm of the inner surface of vessels (Figure 1D), suggesting that new neurons in these regions frequently use blood vessels as migration scaffolds.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy revealed direct attachment of migratory neurons to thin astrocytic endfeet enwrapping blood vessels.
source: Transmission electron microscopy revealed direct attachment of migratory neurons, identified as cells with an elongated cell body, a dark cytoplasm with many free ribosomes, and an electron-dense nucleus with multiple nucleoli (Doetsch et al., 1997), to thin astrocytic endfeet enwrapping blood vessels (Figure 1E), as previously reported in the RMS and GCL (Bovetti et al., 2007; Whitman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and citations to previous studies (Doetsch et al., 1997; Bovetti et al., 2007; Whitman et al., 2009).

claim: Most EGFP+ migrating cells (90.2%) were located within 10 µm of the nearest vessel.
source: Most EGFP+ migrating cells (90.2%) were located within 10 µm of the nearest vessel (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: New neurons were more abundant near high-flow vessels than near low-flow vessels.
source: New neurons were more abundant near high-flow vessels than near low-flow vessels (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: Migration speed was significantly higher in the perivascular region of high-flow vessels than in that of low-flow vessels.
source: Migration speed, as measured by the migration distance of the cell soma, was significantly higher in the perivascular region of high-flow vessels than in that of low-flow vessels (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1I.

claim: The proportion of the migratory period of new neurons in the total imaging period was larger in high-flow perivascular regions than in low-flow regions.
source: The proportion of the migratory period of new neurons in the total imaging period was larger in high-flow perivascular regions than in low-flow regions (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1J.

claim: The maximum migration speed was significantly higher for neurons migrating along high-flow vessels than for those migrating along low-flow vessels.
source: Furthermore, the maximum migration speed, calculated from two consecutive imaging frames, was significantly higher for neurons migrating along high-flow vessels than for those migrating along low-flow vessels (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1K.

claim: Endomucin is downregulated by shear stress on vascular endothelial cells in vitro.
source: To compare the distribution of new neurons in perivascular regions with different blood flows in deep brain regions, we used endomucin, which has been reported to be downregulated by shear stress on vascular endothelial cells in vitro (Zahr et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Zahr et al., 2016).

claim: Endomucin-negative vessels showed higher RBC flow than endomucin-positive vessels.
source: Endomucin-negative vessels showed higher RBC flow than endomucin-positive vessels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), indicating that endomucin can be used as a marker for RBC flow velocity in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The density of BrdU-labeled Dcx+ new neurons was higher in the perivascular region of endomucin-negative vessels than in that of endomucin-positive vessels in the GL, GCL, and RMS.
source: The density of bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU)-labeled doublecortin (Dcx)+ new neurons was higher in the perivascular region of endomucin-negative vessels than in that of endomucin-positive vessels in the GL, GCL, and RMS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–G), suggesting that new neurons migrate along vessels with faster blood flow throughout their migration route.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–G.

claim: The density of perivascular Dcx+/BrdU+ new neurons was significantly higher in SLC16A1-negative perivascular areas than in SLC16A1-positive areas.
source: The density of perivascular Dcx+/BrdU+ new neurons was significantly higher in SLC16A1-negative perivascular areas than in SLC16A1-positive areas (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B), indicating that they actively migrate in the vicinity of arteriole-side vessels (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: A large proportion of Dcx+/BrdU+ new neurons was observed near capillaries in the GL (arterioles; 11.8 ± 2.39%, venules; 4.34 ± 0.212%, capillaries; 83.8 ± 2.25%).
source: A large proportion of Dcx+/BrdU+ new neurons was observed near capillaries in the GL (arterioles; 11.8 ± 2.39%, venules; 4.34 ± 0.212%, capillaries; 83.8 ± 2.25%) (Figure 1M).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1M.

claim: The density of Dcx+/BrdU+ cells was higher near arteriole-side capillaries than that near venule-side capillaries.
source: The density of Dcx+/BrdU+ cells was higher near arteriole-side capillaries than that near venule-side capillaries (Figure 1N).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1N.

claim: In common marmosets, V-SVZ-derived new neurons migrate toward the neocortex and ventral striatum.
source: In common marmosets, but not in mice, V-SVZ-derived new neurons migrate toward the neocortex and ventral striatum (Akter et al., 2020; Figure 1—videos 5 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Akter et al., 2020) and videos (Figure 1—videos 5 and 6).

claim: In the ventral striatum of 3- to 4-month-old common marmosets, Dcx+ immature neurons localized more frequently near SLC16A1-negative vessels than near SLC16A1-positive vessels.
source: In the ventral striatum of 3- to 4-month-old common marmosets, Dcx+ immature neurons localized more frequently near SLC16A1-negative vessels than near SLC16A1-positive vessels, regardless of migration modes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, E.

claim: The density of newly added neurons was significantly higher near high-flow vessels than near low-flow vessels.
source: The density of newly added neurons was significantly higher near high-flow vessels than near low-flow vessels (Figure 1P).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1P.

claim: BrdU-labeled mature neurons were frequently observed in the perivascular region of endomucin-negative vessels.
source: Consistently, BrdU-labeled mature neurons were frequently observed in the perivascular region of endomucin-negative vessels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H.

claim: The proportion of Dcx+/Venus+ cells in the OB was significantly lower in the BCAS group compared with the Sham-operated group at 5 days post injection (dpi).
source: The proportion of Dcx+/Venus+ cells in the OB was significantly lower in the BCAS group compared with the Sham-operated group at 5 days post injection (dpi) (Figure 2B, C), suggesting that blood flow reduction impairs the tangential migration of new neurons in the RMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 2B, C.

claim: BCAS significantly decreased cell proliferation and increased cell death in both the V-SVZ and RMS.
source: BCAS significantly decreased cell proliferation and increased cell death in both the V-SVZ and RMS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that reduced neurogenesis and/or survival may contribute to the decreased distribution of new neurons in the OB.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clot formation resulted in blood flow termination in downstream vessels, which was followed by a decrease in the migration speed of EGFP+ new neurons along downstream vessels.
source: Clot formation resulted in blood flow termination in downstream vessels (Figure 2F), which was followed by a decrease in the migration speed of EGFP+ new neurons along downstream vessels (Figure 2E, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, F, H.

claim: Laser irradiation without rose bengal did not affect the speed of neuronal migration.
source: Laser irradiation without rose bengal did not affect the speed of neuronal migration (Figure 2G), indicating that the inhibition of neuronal migration was not due to laser irradiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by control experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Ghrelin can be delivered from the bloodstream to the brain parenchyma, including the OB tissue, by transcytosis across vascular walls.
source: We focused on ghrelin, which can be delivered from the bloodstream to the brain parenchyma, including the OB tissue, by transcytosis across vascular walls (Rhea et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Rhea et al., 2018).

claim: Newly generated neurons expressed growth hormone secretagogue receptor 1a (GHSR1a), a ghrelin receptor, in the V-SVZ, RMS, and OB.
source: In addition, a previous study showed that newly generated neurons expressed growth hormone secretagogue receptor 1a (GHSR1a), a ghrelin receptor, in the V-SVZ, RMS, and OB (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Li et al., 2014).

claim: Ghsr1a mRNA was detected in Dcx+ new neurons in the V-SVZ, RMS, and OB.
source: Consistent with this report, we detected Ghsr1a mRNA in Dcx+ new neurons in the V-SVZ, RMS, and OB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Migration of V-SVZ-derived new neurons is attenuated in ghrelin knockout mice.
source: A previous study showed that migration of V-SVZ-derived new neurons is attenuated in ghrelin knockout mice (Li et al., 2014), suggesting that ghrelin stimulates neuronal migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Li et al., 2014).

claim: Fluorescently labeled ghrelin accumulated in the RMS and OB after introduction into the bloodstream.
source: We found an accumulation of fluorescent ghrelin in the RMS and OB as reported previously (Rhea et al., 2018; Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and a citation to a previous study (Rhea et al., 2018).

claim: Fluorescence signals of labeled ghrelin were observed in vascular endothelial cells and parenchymal tissue in the RMS and OB.
source: Fluorescence signals were observed in vascular endothelial cells and parenchymal tissue in the RMS and OB (Figure 3B), indicating that blood-derived ghrelin crosses the vascular wall into the brain parenchyma and is delivered to new neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: High levels of fluorescent ghrelin signal were observed in vascular endothelial cells of endomucin-negative, high-flow vessels.
source: In addition, we observed high levels of fluorescent signal in vascular endothelial cells of endomucin-negative, high-flow vessels (Figure 3C, D), which suggests that transcytosis of blood-derived ghrelin may occur more frequently in these vessels, potentially due to increased endothelial endocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D.

claim: The proportion of vessel segments with >1.5-fold increases in ghrelin signal was significantly higher in endomucin-negative vessels than in endomucin-positive ones.
source: The proportion of vessel segments with >1.5-fold increases was significantly higher in endomucin-negative vessels than in endomucin-positive ones (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Vessel segments with >2-fold increases in ghrelin signal were observed exclusively in the endomucin-negative group (6.48% ± 1.18%).
source: Furthermore, vessel segments with >2-fold increases were observed exclusively in the endomucin-negative group (6.48% ± 1.18%).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the analysis.

claim: Ghrelin significantly increased the migration distance of new neurons in V-SVZ cultures.
source: Ghrelin significantly increased the migration distance of these neurons (Figure 4B), indicating enhanced chain migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Ghrelin enhanced the migration speed of control (lacZ-KD) cells.
source: Ghrelin enhanced the migration speed of control (lacZ-KD) cells, indicating that it also facilitates individual migration (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Ghrelin application increased the migratory phase proportion.
source: Ghrelin application increased the migratory phase proportion (Figure 4E) but not the length of the migration cycle (Figure 4F), suggesting that ghrelin signaling elongates the migratory phase of neuronal migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4E, F.

claim: Ghrelin application did not affect the length or speed of leading process extensions.
source: Ghrelin application did not affect the length or speed of leading process extensions (Figure 4G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4G, H.

claim: The somal translocation speed and somal stride length were significantly increased by ghrelin application.
source: In contrast, the somal translocation speed and somal stride length were significantly increased by ghrelin application (Figure 4I, J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4I, J.

claim: No effects of ghrelin were observed in Ghsr1a-KD cells.
source: No such effects were observed in Ghsr1a-KD cells (Figure 4D, E, I, J), suggesting that ghrelin promotes neuronal migration through ghsr1a.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4D, E, I, J.

claim: Ghrelin application extended the duration of actin cup formation.
source: Ghrelin application extended the duration of actin cup formation (Figure 4L) and increased the migration distance during actin cup formation (Figure 4M, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4L, M and video evidence (Figure 4—video 1).

claim: These effects of ghrelin on actin cup formation were not observed in Ghsr1a-KD cells.
source: These effects were not observed in Ghsr1a-KD cells (Figure 4L, M, Figure 4—video 2), suggesting that GHSR1a-mediated ghrelin signaling promotes somal translocation of new neurons by activation of actin cup formation at the rear of the cell soma.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 4L, M and video evidence (Figure 4—video 2).

claim: The percentage of Dcx+ cells reaching the GL was significantly lower in the Ghsr1a-KD group than that in the control group.
source: Of the total labeled Dcx+ cells, the percentage of Dcx+ cells reaching the GL was significantly lower in the Ghsr1a-KD group than that in the control group (Figure 5B, C), suggesting that ghrelin enhances individual radial migration of new neurons in the OB.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5B, C.

claim: Ghsr1a-KD cells showed reduced distribution in the GL compared with that in control cells when lentiviruses were injected into different mice.
source: Consistent with the coinjection results, Ghsr1a-KD cells showed reduced distribution in the GL compared with that in control cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which supports that ghrelin signaling enhances neuronal migration in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When lentiviruses were injected into the V-SVZ, Ghsr1a-KD (DsRed+) cells exhibited decreased distribution in the GL and increased distribution in the RMS compared with control (EmGFP+) cells.
source: When lentiviruses were injected into the V-SVZ (Figure 5D), Ghsr1a-KD (DsRed+) cells exhibited decreased distribution in the GL (Figure 5E, F) and increased distribution in the RMS compared with control (EmGFP+) cells (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5D-H.

claim: There was no significant difference in the proportion of Ki67+ cells in the RMS between control and Ghsr1a-KD groups.
source: Similarly, the percentage of Ki67 + cells in the RMS was similar between the two groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that Ghsr1a-KD does not impair cell proliferation in the RMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant difference in cleaved caspase-3+ cell proportions between control and Ghsr1a-KD groups.
source: We found no significant difference in cleaved caspase-3+ cell proportions between the groups (Control: 874 cells from five mice; Ghsr1a-KD: 678 cells from seven mice), suggesting that ghrelin signaling does not influence the survival of new neurons and their progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the analysis.

claim: BCAS reduced the percentage of Ghsr1a-KD new neurons reaching the OB, similar to the effect seen in control neurons.
source: We found that BCAS reduced the percentage of Ghsr1a-KD new neurons reaching the OB, similar to the effect seen in control neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B, see also Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: Even under Ghsr1a-KD, a higher proportion of new neurons were located in the area of endomucin-negative (high-flow) vessels compared with endomucin-positive (low-flow) vessels.
source: Even under Ghsr1a-KD, a higher proportion of new neurons were located in the area of endomucin-negative (high-flow) vessels compared with endomucin-positive (low-flow) vessels (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C), indicating that Ghsr1a-KD does not abolish the preferential association of migrating neurons with high-flow vessels.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The proportion of labeled cells in the GL was larger in the CR group than in the AL group.
source: The proportion of labeled cells in the GL (Figure 5J) and NeuN+/Dcx− cells among BrdU+ cells in the OB (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B, C) was larger in the CR group than in the AL group.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 4B, C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the proportion of Ghsr1a-KD cells in the GL between the control and CR groups.
source: However, there was no significant difference in the proportion of Ghsr1a-KD cells in the GL between the control and CR groups (Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5K.

claim: There was no significant difference in Ghsr1a expression level in OB Dcx+ cells between the AL and CR groups.
source: We found no significant difference in the Ghsr1a expression level in OB Dcx+ cells between the AL and CR groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Blood vessel-guided cell migration has been reported in various types of cells, including lymphatic endothelial cells in the embryonic zebrafish trunk.
source: Blood vessel-guided cell migration has been reported in various types of cells, including lymphatic endothelial cells in the embryonic zebrafish trunk (Bussmann et al., 2010), Schwann cells, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, glioma cells, and astrocyte progenitors in rodent tissues (Cattin et al., 2015; Farin et al., 2006; Tabata et al., 2022; Tsai et al., 2016), suggesting that it is a common mechanism for efficient cell migration within complex animal tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bussmann et al., 2010; Cattin et al., 2015; Farin et al., 2006; Tabata et al., 2022; Tsai et al., 2016).

claim: Ghrelin, a peripheral hormone produced in the stomach, is delivered to the brain through the bloodstream and accumulates in the brain parenchyma, especially at high levels in the OB.
source: Ghrelin, a peripheral hormone produced in the stomach, is delivered to the brain through the bloodstream and accumulates in the brain parenchyma, especially at high levels in the OB (Rhea et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Rhea et al., 2018).

claim: The ghrelin concentration in blood has been reported to increase during fasting.
source: The ghrelin concentration in blood has been reported to increase during fasting (Toshinai et al., 2001; Tschöp et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Toshinai et al., 2001; Tschöp et al., 2000).

claim: Ghrelin influences neurogenesis in the V-SVZ and subgranular zone of the hippocampal dentate gyrus.
source: In addition to its role in regulating metabolism (Al Massadi et al., 2017; Chopin et al., 2012; Soleyman-Jahi et al., 2019; Stoyanova and Lutz, 2021), ghrelin influences neurogenesis in the V-SVZ and subgranular zone of the hippocampal dentate gyrus (Hornsby et al., 2016; Kent et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Moon et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Hornsby et al., 2016; Kent et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013; Moon et al., 2009).

claim: Ghrelin signaling has been reported to regulate actin cytoskeletal dynamics in astrocytoma cells.
source: Ghrelin signaling has been reported to regulate actin cytoskeletal dynamics in astrocytoma cells (Dixit et al., 2006), which led us to examine whether a similar mechanism operates in migrating neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Dixit et al., 2006).

claim: Somal translocation of migrating cortical interneurons is driven by formation of the actin cup, an accumulation of F-actin at the rear of the cell soma.
source: Somal translocation of migrating cortical interneurons is driven by formation of the actin cup, an accumulation of F-actin at the rear of the cell soma (Martini and Valdeolmillos, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Martini and Valdeolmillos, 2010).

claim: Neural stem cells have been reported to increase blood flow in the adult V-SVZ.
source: Neural stem cells have been reported to increase blood flow in the adult V-SVZ (Lacar et al., 2012), raising the possibility that new neurons may increase blood flow in the OB.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Lacar et al., 2012).

claim: Blood vessel-guided neuronal migration in the adult brain is a conserved phenomenon across species.
source: Because blood vessel-guided neuronal migration in the adult brain is a conserved phenomenon across species (Akter et al., 2020; Kishimoto et al., 2011; Shvedov et al., 2024), we hypothesized that blood flow may also influence neuronal migration in other brain regions of primates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Akter et al., 2020; Kishimoto et al., 2011; Shvedov et al., 2024).

claim: The supply of new neurons to the OB has been suggested to improve olfactory function in food-seeking behavior.
source: Since the supply of new neurons to the OB has been suggested to improve olfactory function in food-seeking behavior (Lazarini and Lledo, 2011), increased neurogenesis caused by long-term CR may contribute to improved olfactory function for food seeking during starvation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Lazarini and Lledo, 2011).

claim: Blood flow promotes the migration of new olfactory-bulb neurons in the adult mammalian brain.
source: Here, we show that blood flow promotes the migration of new olfactory-bulb neurons in the adult mammalian brain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neuronal migration is facilitated by blood flow, leading to accumulation of new neurons near blood vessels with abundant blood flow.
source: Neuronal migration is facilitated by blood flow, leading to accumulation of new neurons near blood vessels with abundant blood flow.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Blood flow inhibition attenuates blood vessel-guided neuronal migration.
source: Blood flow inhibition attenuates blood vessel-guided neuronal migration, suggesting that blood contains factors beneficial to neuronal migration.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from BCAS and photothrombosis experiments.

claim: Ghrelin, which is increased in blood by hunger, directly influences neuronal migration.
source: We found that ghrelin, which is increased in blood by hunger, directly influences neuronal migration.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ghrelin signaling promotes somal translocation by activating actin cytoskeleton contraction at the rear of the cell soma.
source: Ghrelin signaling promotes somal translocation by activating actin cytoskeleton contraction at the rear of the cell soma.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data on actin cup formation.

claim: New neurons mature in the olfactory bulb and contribute to the olfactory function for sensing odorants from food.
source: New neurons mature in the olfactory bulb and contribute to the olfactory function for sensing odorants from food.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about OB neuron function and supported by inference from the experimental context.

claim: Neuronal migration is increased by calorie restriction.
source: Finally, we show that neuronal migration is increased by calorie restriction, and that ghrelin signaling is involved in the process.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from CR experiments.

claim: Ghrelin signaling is involved in the process of increased neuronal migration during calorie restriction.
source: Finally, we show that neuronal migration is increased by calorie restriction, and that ghrelin signaling is involved in the process.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from CR and Ghsr1a-KD experiments.

claim: Blood flow promotes neuronal migration through blood-derived ghrelin signaling in the adult brain, which could be one of the mechanisms that improves the olfactory function for food-seeking behavior during starvation.
source: This study suggests that blood flow promotes neuronal migration through blood-derived ghrelin signaling in the adult brain, which could be one of the mechanisms that improves the olfactory function for food-seeking behavior during starvation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and inference about functional implications.
